The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Let

$$\Sigma:=\{\lambda:\lambda\ \text{is an eigenvalue of}\ T,\ \lambda\ne0\}$$

be its set of nonzero eigenvalues
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]), with eigenspaces
$E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda I)$ for $\lambda\in\Sigma$. Then:

1. $\Sigma$ is a finite or countably infinite set of **real** numbers, each
   eigenvalue has finite multiplicity in the sense $\dim E_\lambda<+\infty$, and
   for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there are only finitely many
   $\lambda\in\Sigma$ with $|\lambda|\ge\varepsilon$; in particular every point
   of $\mathbb F\setminus\{0\}$ has a neighbourhood containing only finitely
   many elements of $\Sigma$, so the only possible accumulation point of
   $\Sigma$ is $0$;
2. the closed linear span $M$ of $\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Sigma}E_\lambda$ satisfies
   $$M=(\ker T)^\perp=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$$
   ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]), and $H=M\oplus M^\perp$
   with $M^\perp\subseteq\ker T$;
3. for every $x\in H$ the finite-subset net of $\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x$
   over the orthogonal projections $P_\lambda$ onto $E_\lambda$ converges in
   norm and
   $$Tx=\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x ;$$
4. if in addition $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, then the nonzero spectrum
   agrees with the nonzero eigenvalues,
   $$\sigma(T)\cap\{\mu\in\mathbb C:\mu\ne0\}=\Sigma .$$

No Hilbert basis of $\ker T$ is selected anywhere: only the orthonormal bases of
the finite-dimensional eigenspaces $E_\lambda$, $\lambda\ne0$, are used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a **self-adjoint positive** trace-class operator
([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-trace-class-operator]]), so that $\langle Tx,x\rangle\ge0$ for every
$x\in H$. Let $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots>0$ be the positive eigenvalues of
$T$ listed with multiplicity
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]) and let
$(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$ be the zero-padded singular-value sequence
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]). Then
$s_n(T)=\lambda_n$ for every $n$, and
$$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n=\|T\|_1 ,$$
where the sum is over the positive eigenvalues with multiplicity and the
equalities are also valid in the finite-rank case (then $\lambda_n:=0$ for
$n$ beyond the rank). This is the positive compact self-adjoint case only; it is
**not** Lidskii's theorem for arbitrary trace-class operators, which is not
claimed here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then:

1. for every **nuclear representation** $Tx=\sum_j\langle x,u_j\rangle v_j$ of
   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. the trace-class operators $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]])
   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. if $T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ and $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$
   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],
   [[def-metric-space]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and for $u,v\in H$ let $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) For every bounded $B\in\mathcal B(H)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]),

$$BT_{u,v}=T_{Bu,v},\qquad T_{u,v}B=T_{u,B^*v},$$

with the Hilbert adjoint $B^*$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class and let $T=\sum_jT_{u_j,v_j}$ be a nuclear representation, i.e. the partial sums converge to $T$ in operator norm and $\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|<\infty$ ([[lem-nuclear-series-characterizes-trace-norm]], [[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then for every bounded $B$

$$\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\sum_j\langle Bu_j,v_j\rangle,\qquad \operatorname{tr}(TB)=\sum_j\langle u_j,B^*v_j\rangle,$$

both series converging absolutely with $\bigl|\operatorname{tr}(BT)\bigr|\le\|B\|\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|$, and $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$ ([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]). In particular $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$ for every trace-class $T$ and bounded $B$, and $\operatorname{tr}(T_{u,v})=\langle u,v\rangle$. No cyclic permutation of unbounded operators is asserted.

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F2], write $\rho=\sum_{j\in J}p_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$, where $J$ is finite or countable, $p_j>0$, and the $u_j$ are orthonormal. The positive-operator trace formula [F3] gives $\sum_jp_j=\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$ and $\|\rho\|_1=1$. For every finite subset $F\subseteq J$, the remainder $\rho-\sum_{j\in F}p_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$ is positive trace class with trace norm $1-\sum_{j\in F}p_j$. Thus these finite partial sums converge to $\rho$ in trace norm as the finite-subset net exhausts $J$; no basis of $\ker\rho$ is used.

By [F5], $\rho A$ is trace class. The trace-norm expansion from step 1.1 is the nuclear representation $\rho=\sum_{j\in J}T_{p_ju_j,u_j}$, since $\sum_j\|p_ju_j\|\|u_j\|=\sum_jp_j=1$. The basis-independent trace [F4] and bounded cyclicity and its nuclear-series formula [F6] give $ \operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_{j\in J}p_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle. $ The series is absolutely convergent because $\sum_jp_j|\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle|\leq\|A\|\sum_jp_j=\|A\|$. Thus $\omega_\rho$ is a well-defined bounded linear functional with $|\omega_\rho(A)|\leq\|A\|$.

For $A=I$, step 2.1 gives $\omega_\rho(I)=\sum_jp_j=1$. If $A\geq0$, every $\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle\geq0$, so step 2.1 gives $\omega_\rho(A)\geq0$. Therefore the trace pairing is a positive normalized bounded functional, as asserted.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $\bigl(x^{(j)}\bigr)_{j\in\mathbb{N}}$
be a sequence in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ whose range
$\{\, x^{(j)} : j \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ is a bounded subset of
$(\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).
Then there are a strictly increasing $i : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
([[def-sequence]], [[lem-index-map-grows]]) and a point $p \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$
with

$$x^{(i_j)} \longrightarrow p \quad \text{in } (\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$$

([[def-metric-convergence]]). By [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]] the same
statement holds with $d_2$ replaced by the metric of any norm on
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$, boundedness and convergence both being unchanged by that
replacement ([[def-equivalent-norms]]).

**This is assembled from published theorems and is not proved again by
bisection.** The bisection is in [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], published at order 120;
what is added here is the passage from compactness to sequential compactness and
the reading of the conclusion in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

**Choice cost: none.** [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] is proved by bisection and uses no
choice principle, and "compact implies sequentially compact" is a theorem of ZF
([[thm-compact-implies-the-other-compactness-forms]]). The five-way equivalence
[[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]] is **not** used, precisely because it is
stated under countable choice and dependent choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]) and
would overcharge this corollary; the arrow-by-arrow account is
[[rem-compactness-choice-ledger-metric]].

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).
If $C$ is at most countable and $m\in\mathbb N$, then the finite product $C^m=\prod_{i<m}C$ is at most countable.

Let $A$ be a nonempty set. Then $A$ is at most countable ([[def-countable]]) if
and only if there is a surjection $s : \mathbb{N} \to A$
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

Moreover, from any such surjection an injection $A \to \mathbb{N}$ is obtained
explicitly, without any choice, by

$$j(a) := \min\{\, k \in \mathbb{N} : s(k) = a \,\}.$$

This is the working form of countability used everywhere below: to prove a
nonempty set countable it suffices to list its elements, repetitions and all.

**No choice principle is used.** The backward direction is where an appeal to
choice would be natural ("for each $a$ pick some $k$ with $s(k) = a$") and it is
avoided outright, because $\min$ is canonical: every nonempty set of naturals has
a *least* element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]), so $j(a)$ is determined by
$a$ and $s$ alone.

The Cauchy-sequence reals $\mathbb{R}_C$ have the **least-upper-bound property**:
every nonempty $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}_C$ that is bounded above has a least upper
bound $\sup S \in \mathbb{R}_C$. Hence, together with [[thm-reals-ordered-field]],
$\mathbb{R}_C$ is a **complete ordered field** ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

derivations.claim: Choose the ordered orthonormal basis of [F3]. In its coordinates $q(u)=\langle Mu,u\rangle$ is a real continuous quadratic polynomial, bounded on the unit sphere by the finite sum of the absolute matrix entries. By [F4], enumerate all rational-coordinate vectors $y_k\in(\mathbb Q+i\mathbb Q)^D$, and put $v_k=y_k/\|y_k\|$ when $y_k\ne0$ and $v_k=e_1$ otherwise. For any unit $x$ and $\varepsilon>0$, coordinatewise rational approximation gives $\|y-x\|<\min(\varepsilon/2,1/2)$ for such a $y$. Then $y\ne0$ and the reverse triangle inequality gives $\|y/\|y\|-x\|\le|1-\|y\||+\|y-x\|\le2\|y-x\|<\varepsilon$. Thus the $v_k$ are dense on the sphere; they are normalizations of rational-coordinate vectors, not necessarily rational-coordinate vectors themselves. The set $S:=\{q(u):\|u\|=1\}$ is nonempty because $e_1$ is a unit vector and is bounded above as just shown; [F5] gives $m:=\sup S\in\mathbb R$. For each $n\ge1$ take the least index $k(n)$ with $q(v_{k(n)})>m-1/n$, which exists by continuity and density. This deterministic rule uses no countable choice. By [F1] the bounded sequence $v_{k(n)}$ has a convergent subsequence; its limit has norm one and attains $m$.

Let $u$ be a maximizing unit vector and $w\perp u$. Differentiating $q((u+tw)/\|u+tw\|)$ at $t=0$ for real $t$ gives $2\operatorname{Re}\langle Mw,u\rangle=0$. Replacing $w$ by $iw$ shows that the imaginary part also vanishes. Hermiticity gives $\langle Mu,w\rangle=0$ for every $w\perp u$, so $Mu=q(u)u$ with real eigenvalue. Moreover $u^\perp$ is invariant, since $\langle Mw,u\rangle=\langle w,Mu\rangle=0$. Induction on $D$, including the one-dimensional case, gives an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues.

For $M=\sum_\lambda\lambda P_\lambda$, define $f(M)=\sum_\lambda f(\lambda)P_\lambda$. The full eigenspaces and their orthogonal projections are intrinsic, so this definition is independent of the basis within each eigenspace. It supplies positive square roots for nonnegative matrices, exponentials for every Hermitian matrix, and the stated logarithm on the positive spectral subspace $S_M$ for every Hermitian $M$: the restriction has exactly the strictly positive eigenvalues. If $S_M=\{0\}$, the empty spectral sum is the unique endomorphism of that zero space. Finite coordinate sums give $\operatorname{Tr}(AB)=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ji}=\operatorname{Tr}(BA)$, hence invariance under unitary changes of orthonormal basis. Diagonalizing $\rho$ gives $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for every complex matrix $A$, and in particular $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho B^*B)=\sum_jp_j\|Bu_j\|^2\ge0$.

Put $a=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$, $b=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho Y^*Y)$ and $c=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*X)$. Step 3.1 gives $c+za+\overline z\,\overline a+|z|^2b\ge0$ for all complex $z$. If $b>0$, take $z=-\overline a/b$ to get $|a|^2\le bc$. If $b=0$, varying $z$ with arbitrarily large magnitude forces $a=0$, giving the same inequality. This proves the stated weighted Cauchy–Schwarz formula (whose form is conjugate-linear in $X$).

The density eigenvalues satisfy $p_j\ge0$ and $\sum_jp_j=1$, so $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)=\sum_jp_j^2\le1$, with equality exactly when one eigenvalue is one and all others vanish. If a rank-one density $\rho=|u\rangle\langle u|$ is $t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $0<t<1$, then every $v\perp u$ has $0=t\langle\sigma v,v\rangle+(1-t)\langle\tau v,v\rangle$. Positivity and the square roots from step 3.1 give $\sigma v=\tau v=0$. Self-adjointness puts their ranges in $\mathbb C u$, and trace one gives $\sigma=\tau=\rho$. Conversely, two positive eigenvalues allow a sufficiently small opposite transfer of weight, yielding distinct densities $\rho_+,\rho_-$ with midpoint $\rho$. Thus precisely the rank-one densities are extreme.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$, the partial
trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B:\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\to
\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_B R)\circ T\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R\circ(T\otimes I_{H_B})\bigr)\quad\text{for every }R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\text{ and }T\in\operatorname{End}(H_A).$$

Here $I_{H_B}$ is the identity map $y\mapsto y$ on $H_B$; $\operatorname{End}$
is the notation defined in [[def-qc-partial-trace]].

Its coordinate formula is independent of the chosen ordered orthonormal basis
of $H_B$. The assertion includes zero-dimensional factors.

Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a separable complex Hilbert space, with inner product linear in its first argument. An operator $\rho\in\mathcal B(H)$ is a **density operator** when it is positive, trace class, and $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. Here trace class means compact with summable singular values, and $\operatorname{Tr}$ is the basis-independent trace of a trace-class operator.

The **normal density state represented by $\rho$** is the functional on bounded operators
$
\omega_\rho(A):=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A),\qquad A\in\mathcal B(H).
$
In this page, “normal density state” means this specified trace-pairing representation; no equivalence with other definitions of normal functionals is assumed. The trace pairing is used only for bounded $A$. Unbounded observables are treated through their spectral probability measures in [[lem-qsm-trace-state-calculus]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Let

$$\Sigma:=\{\lambda:\lambda\ \text{is an eigenvalue of}\ T,\ \lambda\ne0\}$$

be its set of nonzero eigenvalues
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]), with eigenspaces
$E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda I)$ for $\lambda\in\Sigma$. Then:

1. $\Sigma$ is a finite or countably infinite set of **real** numbers, each
   eigenvalue has finite multiplicity in the sense $\dim E_\lambda<+\infty$, and
   for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there are only finitely many
   $\lambda\in\Sigma$ with $|\lambda|\ge\varepsilon$; in particular every point
   of $\mathbb F\setminus\{0\}$ has a neighbourhood containing only finitely
   many elements of $\Sigma$, so the only possible accumulation point of
   $\Sigma$ is $0$;
2. the closed linear span $M$ of $\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Sigma}E_\lambda$ satisfies
   $$M=(\ker T)^\perp=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$$
   ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]), and $H=M\oplus M^\perp$
   with $M^\perp\subseteq\ker T$;
3. for every $x\in H$ the finite-subset net of $\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x$
   over the orthogonal projections $P_\lambda$ onto $E_\lambda$ converges in
   norm and
   $$Tx=\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x ;$$
4. if in addition $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, then the nonzero spectrum
   agrees with the nonzero eigenvalues,
   $$\sigma(T)\cap\{\mu\in\mathbb C:\mu\ne0\}=\Sigma .$$

No Hilbert basis of $\ker T$ is selected anywhere: only the orthonormal bases of
the finite-dimensional eigenspaces $E_\lambda$, $\lambda\ne0$, are used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then:

1. for every **nuclear representation** $Tx=\sum_j\langle x,u_j\rangle v_j$ of
   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$, $K$
and $L$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Then:

1. the trace-class operators $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]])
   form a linear subspace of $\mathcal B(H,K)$ on which $\|\cdot\|_1$ is a norm,
   and
   $$\|T\|\le\|T\|_1\qquad\text{for every }T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$$
   ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. if $T\in\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ and $A\in\mathcal B(K,L)$, $B\in\mathcal B(H_0,H)$
   are bounded linear operators on Hilbert spaces $H_0,L$, then
   $ATB\in\mathcal S_1(H_0,L)$ and
   $$\|ATB\|_1\le\|A\|\,\|T\|_1\,\|B\| ;$$
3. $(\mathcal S_1(H,K),\|\cdot\|_1)$ is a Banach space: every
   $\|\cdot\|_1$-Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ has a limit in
   $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$ to which it converges in $\|\cdot\|_1$
   ([[def-banach-space]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]],
   [[def-metric-space]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
nonzero complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on
$(X,\Sigma)$, and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be bounded and $\Sigma$-measurable
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). Then:

1. there is a unique operator $\Phi_E(f)\in\mathcal B(H)$ with
   $$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,y\rangle=\int f\,dE_{x,y}\qquad(x,y\in H),$$
   and for every sequence $(s_n)$ of complex simple functions with
   $\|f-s_n\|_\infty\to0$ one has $\|\Phi_E(f)-\int s_n\,dE\|\to0$: the integral
   is obtained from uniform simple approximations and is independent of the
   approximating sequence;
2. $\|\Phi_E(f)\|\le\|f\|_\infty$, and for every $x\in H$
$$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,x\rangle=\int f\,dE_x,\qquad \|\Phi_E(f)x\|^2=\int|f|^2\,dE_x ;$$
3. the exact norm is the **$E$-essential supremum**
$$\|f\|_{E,\infty}:=\sup\bigl\{\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}:\ x\in H,\ \|x\|=1\bigr\}, \qquad \|\Phi_E(f)\|=\|f\|_{E,\infty},$$
   where $\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}$ denotes the essential supremum of the real measurable function $|f|$ with respect to
   the finite measure $E_x$ ([[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and for $u,v\in H$ let $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) For every bounded $B\in\mathcal B(H)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]),

$$BT_{u,v}=T_{Bu,v},\qquad T_{u,v}B=T_{u,B^*v},$$

with the Hilbert adjoint $B^*$ ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class and let $T=\sum_jT_{u_j,v_j}$ be a nuclear representation, i.e. the partial sums converge to $T$ in operator norm and $\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|<\infty$ ([[lem-nuclear-series-characterizes-trace-norm]], [[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then for every bounded $B$

$$\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\sum_j\langle Bu_j,v_j\rangle,\qquad \operatorname{tr}(TB)=\sum_j\langle u_j,B^*v_j\rangle,$$

both series converging absolutely with $\bigl|\operatorname{tr}(BT)\bigr|\le\|B\|\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\|$, and $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$ ([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]). In particular $\operatorname{tr}(BT)=\operatorname{tr}(TB)$ for every trace-class $T$ and bounded $B$, and $\operatorname{tr}(T_{u,v})=\langle u,v\rangle$. No cyclic permutation of unbounded operators is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Recall that $T_{u,v}\in\mathcal B(H)$ denotes the rank-one operator $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). If $(u_n)_{n\in J}$ is a finite or countable orthonormal family, with $J$ a finite initial segment of the positive integers or all positive integers, and $w_n\ge0$ with $\sum_nw_n=1$, then the sum $\rho:=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ converges in trace norm to a density operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$. Conversely every density operator $\rho$ admits such an expansion whose weights are its positive eigenvalues counted with multiplicity and whose vectors are orthonormal eigenvectors; distinct expansions of the same $\rho$ exist when a positive eigenspace has dimension at least two.

(b) Let $E$ be a projection-valued measure on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on $H$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]). Then $\mu_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))$ is a well-defined probability measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-probability-measure]]); it is given by the absolutely convergent series $\mu_\rho(B)=\sum_nw_n\|E(B)u_n\|^2$ in every expansion of (a), and reduces to $\mu_\rho(B)=\|E(B)u\|^2$ for a pure density operator $\rho=T_{u,u}$ with $\|u\|=1$.

(c) Assume in addition the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator with projection-valued measure $E_A$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let $\psi\in H$ have $\|\psi\|=1$ and $\psi\in D(A)$. Here $|A|^{1/2}$ denotes the unbounded PVM integral $f(E_A)$ for $f(\lambda)=|\lambda|^{1/2}$, with domain $D(f(E_A))=\{\psi:\int |\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}<\infty\}$ as in [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]. Then

$$\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\|A\psi\|^2 ,$$

where $E_{A,\psi}(B)=\langle E_A(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]); moreover $\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)<\infty$ exactly when $\psi\in D(|A|^{1/2})$, and then the mean $\int\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}$ is finite. No product $A\rho$ of an unbounded operator with a density operator is used, and no physical interpretation of $\mu_\rho$ or of the moments is asserted.

derivations.claim: Since $\rho$ is the trace-one positive density of [F1], [F2] gives $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$, $p_j>0$, with $\sum_jp_j=\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, and trace-norm convergence. For bounded $B$, [F3] makes $\rho B$ trace class. Applying the basis-independent trace to finite partial sums and passing to the trace-norm limit gives $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho B)=\sum_jp_j\langle Bu_j,u_j\rangle$; its absolute sum is at most $\|B\|\sum_jp_j=\|B\|$. The bounded cyclicity statement in [F6] gives $\operatorname{Tr}(B\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho B)$.

The scalar mean is defined on the first absolute-moment domain stated above. If the second moment is finite, then $|\lambda|\le(1+\lambda^2)/2$ and $\mu_\rho$ is a probability measure, so the first absolute moment is finite as well. Expanding $(\lambda-m_\rho(A))^2$ and using $\int1\,d\mu_\rho=1$ gives the displayed variance identity. For a vector $u$, the PVM domain formula [F4] is the operator domain, while the first absolute moment defines the larger form domain $D(|A|^{1/2})=\{u:\int|\lambda|\,dE_u(\lambda)<\infty\}$. These definitions use scalar integrals and make no unbounded cyclic permutation.

Since $0<p_j\leq1$, every term $-p_j\log p_j$ is nonnegative, so the entropy sum is well defined in $[0,\infty]$; multiplying by the given $k_B>0$ preserves that range. It can diverge: let $c^{-1}=\sum_{n\geq2}(n(\log n)^2)^{-1}$ and $p_n=c/(n(\log n)^2)$. The normalizing series converges because the block $2^k\leq n<2^{k+1}$ contributes at most $1/(k\log2)^2$, and $\sum_k k^{-2}$ converges by grouping dyadic blocks. For sufficiently large $n$, $-p_n\log p_n\geq c/(2n\log n)$. Each dyadic block contributes at least $1/(4(k+1)\log2)$ to $\sum_n1/(n\log n)$, so that entropy series diverges.

For each Borel set $C\subseteq\mathbb R$, [F5] and step 1.1 give $\mu_\rho(C)=\sum_jp_j\|E_A(C)u_j\|^2\geq0$ and $\mu_\rho(\mathbb R)=\sum_jp_j=1$. For pairwise disjoint $C_k$, the PVM property gives $\|E_A(\bigcup_k C_k)u_j\|^2=\sum_k\|E_A(C_k)u_j\|^2$, since the projected vectors are orthogonal. The nonnegative double series may be summed in either order; therefore $\mu_\rho(\bigcup_kC_k)=\sum_k\mu_\rho(C_k)$. > Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For a trace-class density $\rho$ with positive eigenvalues $p_i$, define $S(\rho)=-k_B\sum_i p_i\log p_i\in[0,\infty]$, with $0\log0=0$. The logarithm is natural and acts on dimensionless density eigenvalues.

For finite-dimensional densities $\rho,\sigma$, define $\operatorname{supp}\rho=(\ker\rho)^\perp$. If $\operatorname{supp}\rho\not\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\sigma$, set $D(\rho\|\sigma)=+\infty$. Otherwise define
$
D(\rho\|\sigma)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\sigma),
$
where each logarithm is restricted to the positive support of its operator and zero eigenvalues contribute zero to $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)$.

For trace-class normal densities on a separable Hilbert space, write $\rho=\sum_i p_i|u_i\rangle\langle u_i|$ and $\sigma=\sum_j s_j|v_j\rangle\langle v_j|$ on their positive supports. Define the nonnegative cross-log moment
$
C(\rho,\sigma):=\sum_{i,j}p_i(-\log s_j)|\langle u_i,v_j\rangle|^2\in[0,\infty].
$
This is the spectral first moment of $-\log\sigma$ in the scalar state law of $\rho$; equivalently it is the nonnegative sum over the spectral projections, so it is independent of bases within eigenspaces. When support inclusion holds and $C(\rho,\sigma)$ and $S(\rho)$ are both finite, define $D(\rho\|\sigma)=C(\rho,\sigma)-S(\rho)/k_B$. If $C=+\infty$ and $S(\rho)<\infty$, set $D=+\infty$. No value is assigned by this definition to $+\infty-(+\infty)$; [[thm-qsm-trace-cross-log-inequality]] proves that finite $C$ forces finite $S(\rho)$.

Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a separable complex Hilbert space and $\rho$ a trace-class normal density state. Its positive eigenvalues $p_j$ and orthonormal eigenvectors $u_j$ satisfy $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$ in trace norm and $\sum_jp_j=1$. For bounded $A$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$, with absolute value at most $\|A\|$, and $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\operatorname{Tr}(A\rho)$. For a self-adjoint observable $A$ with spectral PVM $E_A$, the scalar law
$
\mu_\rho(B)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho E_A(B))=\sum_jp_j\|E_A(B)u_j\|^2
$
is a probability measure. Its first absolute moment defines a scalar mean, and its second moment defines a variance; these are not defined as arbitrary unbounded products $\rho A$. For a fixed positive Boltzmann scale $k_B>0$ (in SI units J/K), the von Neumann entropy is $S(\rho)=-k_B\sum_jp_j\log p_j\in[0,\infty]$, and need not be finite. Countable convex mixtures of normal density states converge in trace norm.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Assume AC and use the directional convention of
[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. For probability measures $P,Q$ on one
measurable space, $D(P\|Q)\ge0$, and $D(P\|Q)=0$ if and only if $P=Q$.

There is also the following normalized-density identity. Let
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space: it is a set
with a sigma-algebra and measure ([[def-measure-space]]), and there is a
countable measurable cover by sets of finite $\mu$-measure
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]). Let
$\gamma:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable function with
$Z:=\int\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$, and put $\pi=\gamma/Z$. Let
$q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable probability density,
so $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and suppose $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on
$\{\gamma=0\}$. Assume
$$\int q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty,$$
where each term with $q=0$ is defined to be zero. Then
$$\log Z =\int q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu +D(q\,\mu\|\pi\,\mu).$$
In particular, the first integral is at most $\log Z$. This identity concerns
normalized densities only; it does not assert posterior existence for an
unspecified statistical model.

derivations.claim: Write $\rho=\sum_i p_i|u_i\rangle\langle u_i|$ and $\sigma=\sum_j s_j|v_j\rangle\langle v_j|$ on their positive supports. Put $w_{ij}=|\langle u_i,v_j\rangle|^2$, so $\sum_jw_{ij}=1$ because $u_i\in\operatorname{supp}\sigma$, and $\sum_iw_{ij}\leq1$. Define $q_i=\langle\sigma u_i,u_i\rangle=\sum_jw_{ij}s_j>0$; then $Q=\sum_iq_i=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma P_{\operatorname{supp}\rho})\leq1$.

For $q>0$ and $x>0$, $\log x\leq\log q+(x-q)/q$, because $t-1-\log t\geq0$ for $t=x/q$, as its derivative $1-1/t$ has its unique minimum at $t=1$. Applying this tangent inequality to $s_j$ with weights $w_{ij}$ gives $\sum_jw_{ij}(-\log s_j)\geq-\log q_i$. Since $C<\infty$, $T:=\sum_i p_i(-\log q_i)\leq C<\infty$.

For a finite initial set $1\leq i\leq N$, let $a_N=\sum_{i\leq N}p_i$ and $b_N=\sum_{i\leq N}q_i$. Applying the finite-density case of [L1] to $(p_i/a_N)$ and $(q_i/b_N)$ gives $ \sum_{i\leq N}-p_i\log p_i\leq\sum_{i\leq N}p_i(-\log q_i)-a_N\log a_N+a_N\log b_N \leq T-a_N\log a_N, $ because $0<b_N\leq1$. As $N\to\infty$, $a_N\to1$ and $-a_N\log a_N\to0$. The nonnegative partial entropy sums are therefore bounded, so $S(\rho)/k_B=\sum_i-p_i\log p_i<\infty$. This also makes both scalar logarithm series below absolutely defined.

Normalize $q_i$ by $Q$, so $q_i'=q_i/Q$ is a probability distribution with $q_i'>0$. Apply [L1] to $p_i$ and $q_i'$: $\sum_i p_i\log(p_i/q_i')\geq0$, hence $\sum_i p_i\log(p_i/q_i)\geq-\log Q\geq0$. Combining this with the nonnegative Jensen gaps from step 2.1 gives $C-S(\rho)/k_B\geq0$.

Since steps 3.1–4.1 prove that $S(\rho)$ and $T$ are finite, and $q_i'=q_i/Q$, direct logarithm algebra gives $ D(\rho\|\sigma)=C-\frac{S(\rho)}{k_B} =(C-T)+\sum_i p_i\log\frac{p_i}{q_i'}-\log Q. $ The first term is the sum of the nonnegative Jensen gaps from step 2.1, the middle term is the countable relative entropy from [L1], and the last term is nonnegative because $Q\leq1$. If $D(\rho\|\sigma)=0$, all three vanish. Thus $Q=1$; equality in [L1] gives $p_i=q_i'=q_i$ for every $i$. The Jensen gap is $\sum_i p_i\bigl[\sum_jw_{ij}(-\log s_j)+\log q_i\bigr]$; each bracket is nonnegative by step 2.1 and each $p_i>0$, so a zero sum forces equality in every bracket. Strictness of $\log x\leq\log q_i+(x-q_i)/q_i$ then forces $s_j=q_i$ whenever $w_{ij}>0$, and the spectral expansion gives $\sigma u_i=q_i u_i=p_i u_i$. The equality $Q=1$ says $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma(I-P_{\operatorname{supp}\rho}))=0$. Put $P=P_{\operatorname{supp}\rho}$. The spectral expansion and the bounded trace pairing in [F2] give $0=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma(I-P))=\sum_j s_j\|(I-P)v_j\|^2$. Every term is nonnegative and every $s_j>0$, so $(I-P)v_j=0$ for all $j$. Therefore the positive spectral range of $\sigma$ lies in $P H$, and its spectral expansion makes $\sigma$ vanish on $(P H)^\perp$. Therefore $\rho=\sigma$. Conversely, if $\rho=\sigma$, then $q_i=p_i$, $C=S(\rho)/k_B$, and $D=0$.

**Energy-band preparation.** Let $H=H^*$ have spectral PVM $E_H$, and let $P=E_H(B)$ be a nonzero finite-rank projection for a specified Borel energy band $B\subseteq\mathbb R$. When the model declares preparation in this band without additional constraints, adopt the density $\rho=P/\operatorname{Tr}P$. This is a uniform preparation over the finite-dimensional range of $P$; it is not asserted for infinite-rank projections.

**Grand preparation.** Let $\mathcal H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space with a specified nonempty finite or countably infinite orthonormal basis $(u_j)_{j\in J}$, so its finite linear span is dense in $\mathcal H$. For each $\psi=\sum_{j\in J}c_ju_j\in\mathcal H$, define the diagonal self-adjoint energy and particle-number operators by
$$D(H)=\left\{\psi:\sum_j|E_jc_j|^2<\infty\right\},\quad H\psi=\sum_jE_jc_ju_j;\qquad
D(N)=\left\{\psi:\sum_j|n_jc_j|^2<\infty\right\},\quad N\psi=\sum_jn_jc_ju_j,$$
where $E_j\in\mathbb R$ and $n_j\in\mathbb N_0$. For chemical potential $\mu\in\mathbb R$, define the diagonal sum $K_\mu=H-\mu N$ by
$$D(K_\mu)=\left\{\psi:\sum_j|(E_j-\mu n_j)c_j|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad K_\mu\psi=\sum_j(E_j-\mu n_j)c_ju_j.$$
This specifies the self-adjoint operator sum used in this postulate; on $D(H)\cap D(N)$ it agrees with the algebraic difference. Require $\inf_j(E_j-\mu n_j)>-\infty$. Fix $\beta>0$ in J$^{-1}$ and assume
$
0<\Xi(\beta,\mu)=\sum_{j\in J} e^{-\beta(E_j-\mu n_j)}<\infty.
$

$$\operatorname{Cov}_{KM,\rho}(X,Y):=\int_0^1\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^{1-u}\delta X\rho^u\delta Y)\,du.$$

\frac{d}{ds}\log\operatorname{Tr}e^{M(s)}=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_sM'(s)),

> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H,K$ be
nonzero complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$H\widehat\otimes K$ be their completed tensor product with inclusion $\kappa$
([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]). Density operators are
the self-adjoint positive trace-class operators of trace one
([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (a),
[[def-trace-class-operator]]), and for $u,u'\in H$, $v,v'\in K$ the rank-one
operator $T_{u\otimes v,\,u'\otimes v'}$ is the one of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]].

**(a) Product vectors and pure product states.** A vector $\Psi\in
H\widehat\otimes K$ is a **product vector** when $\Psi=\kappa(u\otimes v)$ for
some $u\in H$, $v\in K$. A **pure product state** of the composite is a
density operator of the form
$$T_{\Psi,\Psi},\qquad \Psi=\kappa(u\otimes v),\quad \|u\|=\|v\|=1 .$$
A vector is **non-product** when it is not a product vector.

**(b) Separable states.** Write $\mathcal P$ for the set of all pure product
states, a subset of the set $D(H\widehat\otimes K)$ of density operators. The
**separable states** are the elements of the trace-norm closed convex hull
$$\mathcal S(H,K):=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}\,\mathcal P \ \subseteq\ D(H\widehat\otimes K),$$
where $\operatorname{conv}$ denotes the set of finite convex combinations and
the closure is taken in the trace norm $\|\cdot\|_{1}$ of
[[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]]. A state
$\rho\in D(H\widehat\otimes K)$ is **entangled** (with respect to the
declared splitting $H,K$) when $\rho\notin\mathcal S(H,K)$.

**(c) Conventions and elementary consequences of the form of the definition.**
The set $\operatorname{conv}\mathcal P$ consists exactly of the finite sums
$\sum_{j=1}^{n}w_{j}T_{\Psi_{j},\Psi_{j}}$ with $n\ge1$, weights $w_{j}\ge0$,
$\sum_{j}w_{j}=1$ and unit product vectors $\Psi_{j}$: such sums are convex
combinations of density operators and hence density operators
([[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-density-set-convex-and-complete]] clause (a)),
without any orthogonality requirement on the product vectors.
Every element of $\operatorname{conv}\mathcal P$ is a density operator, and
$\mathcal S(H,K)$ is a convex subset of $D(H\widehat\otimes K)$: if $\rho,\sigma$
are limits of convex combinations $\rho_{n}\to\rho$, $\sigma_{n}\to\sigma$ and
$t\in[0,1]$, then $t\rho+(1-t)\sigma$ is the trace-norm limit of the convex
combinations $t\rho_{n}+(1-t)\sigma_{n}$. Separability of a state is a
property of the declared splitting $(H,K)$; no assertion is made here about
its behaviour under a different factorization of a larger space.

**(d) Finite dimension.** When $H$ and $K$ are finite dimensional,
$\mathcal P$ is compact and $\operatorname{conv}\mathcal P$ is already closed
in the trace norm (it is a compact, hence closed, convex set in the
finite-dimensional space of endomorphisms of $H\widehat\otimes K$), so
$\mathcal S(H,K)=\operatorname{conv}\mathcal P$ and no closure convention is
needed. In the general case the closure in clause (b) is declared explicitly
and is part of the definition.

**(e) Pure-state specialization and status.** A pure state $T_{\Psi,\Psi}$ with $\|\Psi\|=1$ is separable in the precise trace-norm closed-convex-hull sense of clause (b) exactly when $\Psi$ is a product vector of clause (a); otherwise it is entangled. This is the proved mathematical specialization of [[lem-nrqm-composites-pure-state-separability-criterion]], whose locally defined $\mathcal P,\mathcal S$ are exactly those above. Clauses (a)-(e) fix mathematical vocabulary and adopt no physical assumption, dynamics, measurement or probability law. Whether a laboratory preparation realizes a separable or entangled state for the declared splitting remains a tested identification with uncertainty, not a consequence about nature of this definition.

Write $T_{x,y}z=\langle z,y\rangle x$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]. Set
$$\mathcal P=\{T_{\kappa(a\otimes b),\kappa(a\otimes b)}:\|a\|=\|b\|=1\},\qquad \mathcal S=\overline{\operatorname{conv}\mathcal P}^{\|\cdot\|_1},$$
with trace class as in [[def-trace-class-operator]], where the convex hull consists of finite convex combinations, and the closure is taken in the trace-class operators on $L$. For each unit $\Psi\in L$, let $P_\Psi=T_{\Psi,\Psi}$. Then
$$P_\Psi\in\mathcal S\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \Psi=\kappa(a\otimes b)\text{ for some unit }a\in H,\ b\in K.$$

$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

Here trace class means compact with summable singular values, and $\operatorname{Tr}$ is the basis-independent trace of a trace-class operator.

The **normal density state represented by $\rho$** is the functional on bounded operators
$
\omega_\rho(A):=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A),\qquad A\in\mathcal B(H).
$
In this page, “normal density state” means this specified trace-pairing representation; no equivalence with other definitions of normal functionals is assumed. The trace pairing is used only for bounded $A$. Unbounded observables are treated through their spectral probability measures in [[lem-qsm-trace-state-calculus]].

This is the spectral first moment of $-\log\sigma$ in the scalar state law of $\rho$; equivalently it is the nonnegative sum over the spectral projections, so it is independent of bases within eigenspaces. Adopt canonical preparation as follows. Fix the positive Boltzmann constant $k_B>0$ in J/K. For temperature $T>0$, put $\beta=(k_BT)^{-1}$ and adopt
$
\rho_\beta=\frac{e^{-\beta H}}{Z_\beta},\qquad Z_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta H}).
$
In the infinite-dimensional case all scalar energy moments used in a conclusion must also be finite on the actual spectral domain, as required by [[thm-qsm-trace-gibbs-variational]]. With $H$ in joules, $k_B$ in J/K, $T$ in K, and $\beta$ in J$^{-1}$, the exponent is dimensionless and $Z_\beta$ is a dimensionless trace.

This is an adopted preparation rule in the normal-state framework. It is not a theorem that unitary dynamics equilibrates, does not specify a bath or equilibration time, and makes no empirical claim. The finite and trace-Gibbs variational results describe the mathematical optimization associated with this state but do not establish that a physical system is prepared in it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal H\ne\{0\}$ be a separable complex Hilbert space and $A=A^*$ a densely defined Hamiltonian bounded below by $a\in\mathbb R$. Assume $e^{-\beta A}$ is trace class for every $\beta$ in an open interval $I\subset(0,\infty)$. For each $\beta\in I$, put $Z_\beta=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta A})$ and $\rho_\beta=e^{-\beta A}/Z_\beta$. Then $Z_\beta\in(0,\infty)$ and $\rho_\beta$ is a faithful normal density. For the entropy and optimization clause, fix $k_B>0$ (in SI units J/K), put $T=(k_B\beta)^{-1}$ and $F_\beta=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_\beta$, and let $\rho$ be any normal density with finite spectral form energy
$
\mathcal E_A(\rho)=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,d\mu_\rho(\lambda),\qquad
\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,d\mu_\rho(\lambda)<\infty.
$
Then $\rho$ has finite entropy and satisfies
$
\mathcal E_A(\rho)-TS(\rho)\geq F_\beta,
$
with equality exactly at $\rho=\rho_\beta$. The prepared Gibbs state also has
$
S(\rho_\beta)=k_B\bigl(\log Z_\beta+\beta\mathcal E_A(\rho_\beta)\bigr).
$
The trace-class and open-interval hypotheses are essential; a lower bound on $A$ alone does not imply finite $Z_\beta$.

derivations.claim: Let $\lambda_n=\hbar\omega(n+\tfrac12)$. Finite-support vectors lie in $D(H)$, so the domain is dense. Since each $\lambda_n$ is real, the diagonal operator is symmetric. If $y\in D(H^*)$, there is $z\in\ell^2$ such that $\langle Hc,y\rangle=\langle c,z\rangle$ for every $c\in D(H)$. Testing $c=e_n$ gives $z_n=\lambda_ny_n$, so $(\lambda_ny_n)\in\ell^2$, which is exactly $y\in D(H)$. Conversely, if this sequence is square summable, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\langle Hc,y\rangle=\langle c,(\lambda_ny_n)\rangle$ for every $c\in D(H)$. Thus $D(H^*)=D(H)$ and $H^*=H$.

The diagonal exponential has eigenvalues $e^{-x(n+1/2)}$. The finite geometric sum identity and $r^n\to0$ give $\sum_{n\geq0}r^n=(1-r)^{-1}$, so $Z_\beta=e^{-x/2}/(1-r)<\infty$. Set $E_*:=\hbar\omega>0$ in J. For any compact inverse-energy interval $[b,B]\subset(0,\infty)$, the dimensionless terms $[1+(\lambda_n/E_*)^2]e^{-\beta\lambda_n}$ are bounded by $[1+(n+\tfrac12)^2]e^{-bE_*(n+1/2)}$. The ratio of consecutive terms of this last series tends to $e^{-bE_*}<1$, so it is summable. Since $y\leq1+y^2$ for $y\geq0$, this gives finite trace and first and second energy moments after multiplying the corresponding bounds by $E_*$ or $E_*^2$. Hence [F1] and [F2] make $\rho_\beta$ a normal density, and [F4] identifies it with the adopted canonical preparation.

The normalized weights are $p_n=(1-r)r^n$. Absolute convergence permits subtracting the two convergent series to get $(1-r)\sum_{n\geq0}nr^n=\sum_{n\geq1}r^n=r/(1-r)$; therefore $\sum n p_n=r/(1-r)$. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces,

$$\lVert ST\rVert\le \lVert S\rVert\,\lVert T\rVert.$$

For every such linear map $T$,

$$\lVert T^*T\rVert=\lVert T\rVert^2.$$

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and assume
$X$ admits an ordered basis of finite length. Then $X$ is a Banach space in the
sense of [[def-banach-space]].
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

For indices $a,b$ in the same finite index set, the **Kronecker delta** is

$$\delta_{ab}:=\begin{cases}1,&a=b,\\0,&a\ne b.\end{cases}$$

Let $i<m$ and $j<n$. The **matrix unit** $E_{ij}\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ is the
matrix whose $(r,s)$-entry is

$$(E_{ij})_{rs}:=\delta_{ri}\delta_{sj}.$$

Thus $E_{ij}$ has entry $1$ in position $(i,j)$ and entry $0$ everywhere else.
When a dimension is zero, no index of that dimension exists and there are no
matrix units of the corresponding shape.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

A **possibly nonunital complex Banach algebra** is a complex vector space $A$
equipped with an associative complex-bilinear multiplication
$A \times A \to A$ ([[def-bounded-bilinear-map]] for the bilinearity convention)
and a norm under which $A$ is a Banach space ([[def-banach-space]],
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]), such that the norm is
**submultiplicative**:

$$\|ab\| \le \|a\|\,\|b\| \qquad (a,b \in A).$$

No multiplicative identity is assumed, and no real-algebra or unital
convention is imported from elsewhere.

A **complex C\*-algebra** is a possibly nonunital complex Banach algebra $A$
equipped with an **involution** $A \to A$, $a \mapsto a^*$, which is
conjugate-linear ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) and
satisfies

$$(a^*)^* = a, \qquad (ab)^* = b^*a^*, \qquad \|a^*a\| = \|a\|^2 \qquad (a,b \in A).$$

The last identity is the **C\*-identity**. Two immediate consequences are worth
recording, and both are proved from the displayed axioms alone:

- **the involution is isometric**: $\|a^*\| = \|a\|$. Indeed $\|a\|^2 = \|a^*a\| \le \|a^*\|\,\|a\|$ gives $\|a\| \le \|a^*\|$ when $a \ne 0$, and applying this inequality to $a^*$ and using $(a^*)^* = a$ gives $\|a^*\| \le \|a\|$; the case $a = 0$ is trivial;
- **no norm-uniqueness assertion is part of this definition**: such a theorem
  needs additional hypotheses and proof, and does not follow merely by naming
  the displayed C\*-identity.

Let $A$ and $B$ be complex C\*-algebras. A **bounded star-homomorphism**, or
bounded $*$-homomorphism, is a bounded complex-linear map
$\varphi : A \to B$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) satisfying

$$\varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b), \qquad \varphi(a^*) = \varphi(a)^* \qquad (a,b \in A).$$

A star-homomorphism is **not** required to be unital, and it is not required
that a unit be present or preserved; when $A$ and $B$ both happen to be unital,
$\varphi$ is called **unital** if $\varphi(1_A) = 1_B$. The bounded nonunital
star-homomorphisms are the arrows of the locally compact duality theorem on this
page ([[thm-locally-compact-gelfand-duality]]), with properness imposed there
through [[def-approximate-unit-and-proper-c-star-morphism]].

Let $A$ be a complex C\*-algebra ([[def-c-star-algebra]]) and recall that
positivity in $A$ is the algebraic condition $a=b^*b$, without spectral
hypotheses ([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-elements-of-a-c-star-algebra]]).
A linear functional $\omega:A\to\mathbb C$ is **positive** if
$$\omega(a^*a)\ge0\qquad\text{for every }a\in A,$$
and a **state** if in addition $\|\omega\|=1$, the norm being the operator
norm of the bounded linear functional on $A$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

derivations.claim: Choose an ordered orthonormal basis $e_1,\ldots,e_D$. Its matrix units form an ordered basis of the complex endomorphism space, since $A=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}E_{ij}$ uniquely. The operator norm is a norm: its triangle inequality and homogeneity follow by applying the vector norm to $Av$ for unit $v$, and norm zero implies $Ae_j=0$ for all $j$. Matrix composition is associative and complex bilinear, and conjugate transpose is conjugate-linear, involutive and reverses products. By [F2] the norm is submultiplicative, complete, and satisfies $\|A^*A\|=\|A\|^2$. Thus all axioms of [F4] hold. The identity is nonzero and has norm one because $D\ge1$. The C*-identity and submultiplicativity give $\|A\|^2\le\|A^*\|\|A\|$, and applying this also to $A^*$ gives $\|A^*\|=\|A\|$, including $A=0$.

For every vector $v$, $\langle(\|A\|^2I-A^*A)v,v\rangle=\|A\|^2\|v\|^2-\|Av\|^2\ge0$. This Hermitian matrix is positive semidefinite, so [F1] gives its positive square root. The same spectral calculus shows that matrix positivity is equivalent to being $B^*B$, agreeing with the algebraic positivity used in [F4].

Let $\omega$ be complex linear and positive, and define $\rho_{ij}:=\omega(E_{ji})$. Finite expansion gives $\omega(A)=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}\omega(E_{ij})=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)$. For a column vector $z$, take $B=e_1z^*$; then $B^*B=zz^*$, so $z^*\rho z=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho zz^*)=\omega(B^*B)\ge0$ is real. Substitution of $z=e_i$, $e_i+e_j$, and $e_i+i e_j$ shows that the diagonal is real and $\rho_{ji}=\overline{\rho_{ij}}$; hence $\rho$ is Hermitian and its nonnegative quadratic forms make it positive semidefinite. Taking $A=I$ gives $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=\omega(I)$. The formula on the matrix units forces every entry of any representing matrix, proving uniqueness.

Conversely let $\rho\ge0$ and diagonalize it by [F1] as $\rho=\sum_j p_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$, $p_j\ge0$. Then $\omega_\rho(A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ is complex linear and $\omega_\rho(B^*B)=\sum_jp_j\|Bu_j\|^2\ge0$. For every complex $A$, vector Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\omega_\rho(A)|\le\sum_jp_j\|Au_j\|\le(\sum_jp_j)\|A\|$. Thus its functional norm is at most $\operatorname{Tr}\rho$, and evaluating at the norm-one identity gives the reverse inequality. This proves the norm formula, including $\rho=0$. The preceding reconstruction and this converse give the full bijection; imposing norm one is exactly imposing trace one by [F4], with no faithfulness requirement.
